cues.text: A Friendship That Shaped a Life
Born around 329 near Nazianzus in Cappadocia, Gregory was the son of a bishop and a devoutly Christian mother.
He received an outstanding education at Caesarea, Alexandria, and finally Athens.
There, he formed with fellow Cappadocian student Basil , later called the Great, a friendship so deep that Gregory would later describe them as sharing, in effect, a single soul in two bodies.
Gregory's own deepest longing throughout his life was for the quiet of monastic retirement and theological study.
This temperament sits movingly beside the record of a man repeatedly called out of that quiet into the most turbulent controversies of his age.
Pressed Into Ministry Against His Will

Gregory's own father, aging and in need of help, ordained his reluctant son a priest almost by surprise; Gregory, overwhelmed, fled temporarily to join Basil's monastic community before his conscience brought him back to assist his father's diocese.
This pattern — genuine reluctance overcome, again and again, by a deeper sense of duty to friends and to the Church — would repeat itself across Gregory's public life.
It never did so because he sought advancement, but because someone he could not refuse had asked something of him that he alone seemed equipped to give.
A Congregation in a Single House
In 379, at the urgent request of Basil and the sorely persecuted Nicene faithful of Constantinople , Gregory reluctantly agreed to travel there.
The city had been almost entirely in Arian hands for decades, and he agreed to take up their spiritual care.
He began with nothing more than a single house, converted into a small chapel he called Anastasia, “Resurrection.”
It was a fitting name, since Nicene orthodoxy would, within two years, rise again from this humble beginning.
It would become the faith publicly professed throughout the imperial capital.
It was in this same small chapel that Gregory delivered, in the course of 380, the five Theological Orations on which his lasting fame chiefly rests.

They offered a sustained, luminous defense of the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit, so precise and eloquent that the Council of Chalcedon , seventy years later, would formally confer on Gregory the title "the Theologian."
This was an honor the Church had given, until then, only to the Apostle John .
A Council, and a Swift Resignation
When the Council of Constantinople gathered in 381 to confirm decisively the Nicene faith Gregory had defended so eloquently, he was named its president.
He was also confirmed as the city's rightful bishop—the very vindication his years of patient, unwanted labor might have seemed to deserve.
Yet almost immediately, disputes arose among the assembled bishops over the legitimacy of his own appointment, disputes rooted more in ecclesiastical politics than in any fault of Gregory's own.
Rather than allow the council's urgent doctrinal work to be overshadowed by controversy over his own person, Gregory did something remarkably rare in the history of ambitious churchmen.
He resigned the office he had been given in a farewell address of moving humility, then withdrew at last to the quiet he had longed for throughout his entire public life.
A Quiet End
Gregory spent his remaining years at his family's estate near Nazianzus, in the retirement he had always craved.
He wrote poetry — including a remarkable autobiographical poem recounting his own life and struggles — and continued his theological correspondence until his death around 390.
Legacy
The Church still recites, at Sunday and solemnity Masses, the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed.
Gregory's Theological Orations did so much to secure and clarify its confession of the Trinity.
The Eastern Church still honors him, alongside Basil and John Chrysostom, as one of its Three Holy Hierarchs.
Gregory's own life, torn continually between contemplative solitude and the urgent needs of a Church in crisis, remains a companion for every believer who has felt that tension.
It reminds us that the deepest theology is very often written not by those who sought public honor, but by those who accepted it reluctantly.
They did so only because love for the truth and for their friends left them, in the end, no other choice.
